objectives: Compare how government tools for reducing negative externalities work (command-and-control regulation, pollution and carbon taxes, emissions trading, and property rights) and weigh their strengths and weaknesses.

Calculate how a per-unit carbon tax affects the consumer price, the producer price, quantity, tax revenue, and emissions, and explain how the tax burden is split according to how sensitive demand and supply are to price.
Evaluate a tax rate by calculating the change in social welfare including external damage, and discuss the effects, fairness, and limits of a carbon tax from the perspective of SDG 7 and SDG 13.

concepts.definition: An approach in which the government sets allowable pollution levels or required technologies and makes everyone meet the same standard. The result is clear, but firms have no incentive to cut beyond the standard, and the rule cannot account for differences in abatement costs across firms.

A tax charged on each unit of pollution that builds the external cost into the price. Each firm cuts pollution wherever cutting is cheaper than paying the tax, so reductions happen first where they are easiest.

A pollution tax applied to emissions of greenhouse gases such as carbon dioxide. Like emissions trading, it puts a price on carbon, and its revenue can be used to support households or fund clean investment.

An approach in which the government sets a cap on total emissions, hands out emissions permits (rights to emit), and lets firms buy and sell them. The government fixes the total, and trading decides who cuts how much.
Who actually bears the burden of a tax. Regardless of who is legally required to pay it, the side that is less sensitive to price bears more of it.

When a tax reduces trade, some gains from trade within the market are lost (deadweight loss), but external damage is avoided on every unit no longer traded. A policy can be evaluated only by looking at both effects together.

beginner.summary: When pollution has a price, people cut it on their own. A carbon tax puts a price on greenhouse gases. Prices go up, people buy less, firms make less, and emissions fall.

sections.heading: Different ways to reduce pollution
paragraphs: Governments have several ways to cut pollution. They can set a rule such as no factory may release more than a certain amount of smoke, and make everyone follow it (command-and-control regulation). They can set a limit on total emissions and let firms buy and sell the right to emit (an emissions trading system, also called cap-and-trade). Or they can put a price on pollution.

sections.heading: Putting a price on pollution
paragraphs: If a firm has to pay a tax every time it pollutes, it compares the cost of cutting pollution with the tax. Firms that can cut cheaply cut a lot, and firms that find it hard to cut pay the tax. A tax that builds the harm from pollution into the price is called a pollution tax, and a pollution tax on greenhouse gases is called a carbon tax.

sections.heading: Who pays, and how much?
paragraphs: Even if the carbon tax is charged to firms, firms do not carry the whole burden. Prices go up, so consumers pay part of it too. If people need the product even when the price rises, consumers carry more of the burden. If people can easily switch to something else, firms carry more.

sections.heading: A tax is not only a loss
paragraphs: When a tax reduces trade, some of the gains people got from buying and selling are lost. But pollution falls too, so people avoid some harm. If the harm avoided is bigger than the gains lost, society as a whole comes out ahead.

The carbon-tax experiment in the 'Interactive simulation' section further down this lesson starts with a = 100, b = 2, c = 10, d = 1, a tax of t = 6, external damage md = 6, and emissions e = 1. These are the same values used in worked examples 1 to 3. Try raising the tax t step by step from 0 and watch how 'Price paid by consumers', 'Quantity after tax', and 'Emissions (after tax)' change. These starting values are simplified hypothetical numbers chosen to show how a carbon tax works, not real carbon prices. Read every result in the units of the model ($ per unit of the good, kg of emissions per unit), and do not use them to guess what a real carbon tax costs.

intermediate.summary: A per-unit carbon tax shifts the supply curve up by the amount of the tax. The price consumers pay rises, the price producers receive falls, quantity and emissions drop, and the government collects tax revenue.

sections.heading: Regulation versus prices: what is the difference?
paragraphs: Command-and-control regulation applies the same standard to every firm, so the result is clear. But once a firm meets the standard, it has no incentive to cut further, and the rule cannot account for differences in abatement costs across firms. A pollution tax sets the price and lets firms decide how much to cut, while an emissions trading system sets the total amount and lets trading determine the price. Both market-based tools make reductions happen first where abatement is cheapest, so they achieve the same reduction at a lower total cost.

sections.heading: A carbon tax on the graph
paragraphs: A per-unit tax t charged to producers shifts the supply curve up by t (from S to S+t). At the new equilibrium, the price consumers pay rises, and the price producers keep after paying the tax falls. The gap between the two prices is t. Quantity falls, so emissions fall too, and the government collects revenue equal to the tax times the quantity.
How the tax splits between a higher consumer price and a lower producer price depends on how sensitive demand and supply are to price. The side that is less sensitive to price bears more of the tax.

sections.heading: Lost gains from trade versus avoided damage
paragraphs: When a tax reduces trade, part of the gains from trade that would exist without any externality disappears (the loss within the market, or deadweight loss). But when there is an external cost, every unit no longer traded avoids damage equal to that external cost. Change in social welfare = avoided external damage − loss within the market.

The carbon-tax experiment in the 'Interactive simulation' section further down this lesson starts with a = 100, b = 2, c = 10, d = 1, a tax of t = 6, external damage md = 6, and emissions e = 1. These are the same values used in worked examples 1 to 3. Compare the rows 'Consumer burden (per unit)', 'Producer burden (per unit)', 'Tax revenue', 'Avoided external damage (assumed)', and 'Change in social welfare (assumed)' in the results table with your calculations from worked examples 1 to 3. Then change the demand slope b and see how the consumer share of the tax changes. Keep the units consistent: t and md are dollars per unit of the good, and e is kilograms of emissions per unit, so a tax of $6 per unit with e = 1 kg is $6 per kilogram of emissions. That is far higher than real carbon prices, which are usually quoted per tonne of carbon dioxide. The default values are chosen to make the mechanism easy to see, not to represent any real tax rate.

advanced.summary: A tax rate t reduces quantity by ΔQ = b·d·t/(b + d). If the external damage per unit is md, the welfare change is ΔQ·(md − t/2), which is largest at t = md (the Pigouvian tax).

sections.heading: Comparing policy tools
paragraphs: Firms differ in their marginal cost of reducing pollution. Under a pollution tax, each firm cuts until its marginal abatement cost equals the tax, so every firm ends up with the same marginal abatement cost, and any given reduction is achieved at the lowest possible cost. In an emissions trading system, the permit price plays the same role. The difference lies in uncertainty: a tax fixes the price (the cost of abatement) and leaves the amount of reduction uncertain, while an emissions trading system fixes the amount of reduction and leaves the price uncertain. A tax may suit cases with a very large number of emission sources to monitor, while permits may suit cases with few sources where the total amount matters most.

sections.heading: The effects of the tax in equations
paragraphs: With demand Qd = a − bP and supply Qs = c + d(P − t), the consumer price is Pc = (a − c + d·t)/(b + d) and the producer price is Pp = Pc − t. If P* is the equilibrium price with no tax, the consumer burden is Pc − P* = t·d/(b + d) and the producer burden is P* − Pp = t·b/(b + d). The less sensitive demand is to price (the smaller b is), the larger the consumer share d/(b + d).
Reduction in quantity ΔQ = b·d·t/(b + d), tax revenue = t·(Q* − ΔQ), and change in emissions = e·ΔQ (where e is emissions per unit).

sections.heading: The optimal tax rate: the Pigouvian tax
paragraphs: The loss within the market (deadweight loss) is ½·t·ΔQ, and if the external damage per unit is md, the avoided damage is md·ΔQ. So the change in social welfare is W(t) = ΔQ·(md − t/2) = k·t·(md − t/2), where k = b·d/(b + d). Differentiating W with respect to t gives k·(md − t), so W is largest when t = md. A tax rate equal to the external cost is called a Pigouvian tax, after the economist Arthur Pigou, who proposed taxing polluters by the amount of harm they cause others. When t is twice md, W = 0, and any higher rate actually lowers welfare.

A caution: this model assumes straight-line demand and supply and a constant damage per unit. In reality, estimates of the social cost of carbon are uncertain, and lower-income households may feel the burden more heavily, so how the revenue is used shapes both the fairness of the policy and how willing people are to accept it.

The carbon-tax experiment in the 'Interactive simulation' section further down this lesson starts with a = 100, b = 2, c = 10, d = 1, a tax of t = 6, external damage md = 6, and emissions e = 1. These are the same values used in worked examples 1 to 3. Set t to 3, 6, and 12 in turn, record the 'Change in social welfare (assumed)' each time, and compare the results with the formula for W(t). Then change md and check where the t that gives the largest welfare change moves. Unit check: with t in dollars per unit and e in kilograms per unit, the implied price of emissions is t ÷ e dollars per kilogram, or 1,000 × t ÷ e dollars per tonne. The default values (t = 6, e = 1) imply $6,000 per tonne, which is a teaching number, not a realistic carbon price. Real-world carbon prices and estimates of the social cost of carbon are measured per tonne of carbon dioxide and are uncertain, so compare mechanisms, not magnitudes.

worked_examples.title: How much does a carbon tax raise the price?
worked_examples.problem: Hypothetical example: In a market, demand is Qd = 100 − 2P and supply is Qs = 10 + P. With no tax, the equilibrium price is $30 and the equilibrium quantity is 40. If producers are charged a carbon tax of $6 per unit, the price consumers pay becomes $32. How much did the consumer price rise, and what price do producers keep after paying the tax?
steps: Price producers keep = consumer price − tax = $32 − $6 = $26.
worked_examples.answer: The consumer price rose by $2, and the price producers keep fell by $4, to $26. Of the $6 tax, consumers bear $2 and producers bear $4.

worked_examples.title: Quantity, tax revenue, and emissions
worked_examples.problem: Hypothetical example (the market from worked example 1): After the $6 tax, what are the quantity and the tax revenue? If making one unit releases 1 kg of greenhouse gases, by how much do emissions fall? Who bears more of the tax, and why?
steps: Quantity after the tax = 100 − 2 × 32 = 36 (the same as on the supply side: 10 + 26 = 36).
Emissions: 40 kg before the tax and 36 kg after, a drop of 4 kg.
Burden shares: consumers d/(b + d) = 1/3 and producers b/(b + d) = 2/3. In this market, supply is less sensitive to price than demand (d = 1 < b = 2), so producers bear more.
worked_examples.answer: Quantity is 36, tax revenue is $216, and emissions fall by 4 kg. Because supply is less sensitive to price, producers bear 2/3 of the tax.

worked_examples.title: Evaluating welfare with external damage
worked_examples.problem: Hypothetical example (the market from worked example 1): Assume each unit causes $6 of external damage. With a $6 tax, find the loss within the market, the avoided external damage, and the change in social welfare. What happens if the tax rises to $12?
steps: t = 6: reduction in quantity ΔQ = 40 − 36 = 4. Loss within the market = ½ × 6 × 4 = $12; avoided damage = 6 × 4 = $24.
Change in social welfare = $24 − $12 = +$12 (matching the formula ΔQ·(md − t/2) = 4 × (6 − 3) = 12).
t = 12: Pc = (90 + 12)/3 = $34, quantity = 100 − 68 = 32, ΔQ = 8. Loss within the market = ½ × 12 × 8 = $48; avoided damage = 6 × 8 = $48, so the welfare change is $0.
The welfare change is largest when the tax rate equals the external damage (t = md = 6), and the gain disappears when the rate doubles to 12.
worked_examples.answer: At t = 6, social welfare rises by $12. At t = 12, the avoided damage and the loss within the market are both $48, so the welfare change is $0.

graphs.title: The effect of a $6 carbon tax
graphs.caption: Hypothetical example (worked examples 1 to 3; same as the simulation starting values). The $6 tax shifts the supply curve up from S to S+t. Consumer price $32, producer price $26, quantity falls from 40 to 36. The $6 tax is a teaching value in the model units, not a real carbon price.

real_world_examples.title: The limits of command-and-control regulation
paragraphs: Laws that set allowable emissions or required equipment have long been criticized because they give firms no incentive to cut further once they meet the standard, and because they treat firms that could cut a lot at low cost the same as firms that cannot.

real_world_examples.title: An example of emissions trading
paragraphs: Through the 1990 amendments to the Clean Air Act, the United States capped sulfur dioxide emissions from power plants and allowed the emission permits to be traded. Market-based tools let firms find the cheapest ways to cut emissions on their own.

real_world_examples.title: Carbon pricing and the use of revenue
paragraphs: The International Monetary Fund (IMF) sees carbon pricing, such as carbon taxes and emissions trading systems, as a central tool for mitigating climate change. It explains that using the revenue to support lower-income households, or to help households and businesses switch to clean technology, makes the policy easier for the public to accept.

sdg_case.title: How should carbon tax revenue be used?
paragraphs: SDG target 13.2 calls for integrating climate change measures into national policies, and SDG 7 aims for affordable (7.1) and clean (7.2) energy for everyone, along with better energy efficiency (7.3).

Hypothetical situation: A country has introduced a carbon tax, which brings in revenue every year. Because the tax raises energy prices, households that spend a large share of their income on energy may feel the burden heavily. The government has to choose how to use the revenue. The numbers in this lesson and its simulation are hypothetical teaching values, so they do not tell you how large a real carbon tax or its revenue would be.

options.name: Return the revenue to every resident in equal amounts (sometimes called a carbon dividend)
benefits: Lower-income households may get back more than they pay in higher prices, which helps with fairness.
The price signal stays in place, so emissions keep falling.
costs: No money is left for renewable energy investment.
Sending out the payments has administrative costs.
assumptions: Households keep choosing to use less energy even after they receive the payments.

options.name: Invest in renewable energy and energy efficiency (SDG 7.2 and 7.3)
benefits: The supply of clean energy grows, lowering emissions and energy costs over the long run.
It strengthens the positive externalities of clean technology.
costs: It does not ease the burden on households right away.
The investment takes a long time to pay off.
assumptions: The investment is carried out efficiently, and technology costs keep falling.

options.name: Help lower-income households with energy costs (SDG 7.1)
benefits: It directly helps the households that carry the heaviest burden.
It may reduce opposition to the policy.
costs: The eligibility rules and administration can be complicated.
If support is tied to energy use, the incentive to save energy may weaken.
assumptions: Support is based on income, not on how much energy a household uses.

discussion: If a carbon tax has two goals, cutting emissions and fairness, how should the three options be combined? Support your answer with the tax revenue and consumer burden you saw in the simulation.

key_takeaways: Command-and-control regulation gives clear results but little flexibility, while pollution taxes and emissions trading systems make reductions happen first where abatement is cheapest (a tax sets the price; permits set the total amount).

A per-unit carbon tax raises the consumer price and lowers the producer price, which reduces quantity and emissions and generates tax revenue. The side that is less sensitive to price bears more of the tax.

When there is external damage, a tax is judged by avoided damage minus the loss within the market. In a straight-line model, this is largest when the tax rate equals the external damage per unit. How the revenue is used shapes fairness.
